tags.gist: Says least-burdensome principles and timely access must not displace FDA's core mandate of reasonable assurance of safety and effectiveness.
Sees the GenAI framework as a chance to strengthen evidence standards generally, given 510(k) reliance on surrogates and limited datasets.
Wants prospective clinical studies as the principal evidence for devices directly influencing care, since benchmarks miss human variability, misinterpretation, system effects and emergent risks.
Calls evaluator judgments of outputs a surrogate for clinical performance whose link to outcomes is unproven, so benchmark results deserve caution.
Says the breadth of GenAI devices is no reason to abandon prospective evaluation where meaningful clinical endpoints exist.
For devices with discrete outcomes, such as insulin-dosing advice, wants a non-inferiority clinical study on outcomes like glycemic control rather than expert rating of text.
For broad-scope devices, pairs patient outcomes with independent adjudication of real cases, doubting retrospective or shadow methods capture interactive use.
Wants a low threshold for prospective evaluation, with action-directing and action-taking devices getting prospective scrutiny regardless of consequence level.
Would let benchmarking and simulation support clearance only of lower-risk informational devices, never establish safety where use affects patient care.
Warns that leaning on benchmarks, surrogates and machine assessment risks detaching regulation from the outcomes that matter to patients.
